title: Learning instruments without lessons; Happy Schilling and Gussie Mueller
summary: Secondhand instruments, Schilling leaving instruments at the house, Tom and Ted teaching themselves bass and trombone; Ray Lopez and Mueller.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the horn: first instrument and the trombone

blocks.x: Did they use any of these homemade instruments with those groups or did they use all regular instruments?

Well, at that particular time, they were, these boys had all batted up instruments, you know, maybe they bought, the majority of them bought them second handed. They couldn't afford to buy the new ones. They were too expensive for them. And later on, as they played, they played a lot of jobs while they got new instruments. But they were pretty high in those days. The instruments weren't so plentiful as they are today. And when we got an old batted instrument, we tried to repair it the best way we could and learn how to play something on it. Now we had what we call a fissured band around in New Orleans. One of the boys, by the name of Schilling, did you meet him? Happy? Yeah. Happy Schilling, yes. That's the one, yeah. Well, he's largely responsible for us playing. Tom and I, we decided to go batting at one time. And we read at the house and we furnished it. And the happy Schilling used to come over there and ask permission at different times to leave a lot of instruments over there. Trombone, tubas, clarinets, you know, different band instruments. Oh, we were tickling to death and let them leave it over there because Tom and I used to fool around with them during the day. And before we knew it, we knew how to play a lot of them, see. We just, out of curiosity, wanted to see if we could play them. We applied ourselves enough and sure enough we learned how to play. I played a little bit on the clarinet, the cornet, trombone, tubas, things like that. And Tom did the same thing. Well, Tom seemed to love trombone and I loved the bass more than I loved any other instrument. And we used to sit down at the piano, you know, and play, learn to play quite a few numbers on piano. And while we liked all the instruments, still the bass seemed to appeal to me. It seemed like I loved that instrument. And Tom seemed to love the trombone more than any other instrument too. So we, we stopped playing so well that we attracted attention and people started hiring us for different dances. No lessons on them.

No lessons on anything. In fact, we had trumpet player Ray Lopez, he played the, his cornet, as I call it, because he was short, see. Left handed. Instead of right handed, he put his left hand over the horn and figured that way, left handed. Well, that was his style of playing. But he wasn't taught. The only one that knew how to read a few notes was Gussie Mueller. And he could only read the lead part on top of a piano part. And he'd play that over and we'd catch it just that quick, see, and we'd form our own harmony and rhythm to it. And that's the way we learned our numbers.
Now what was your first instrument that you took up?

Your very first one. Oh I strummed on guitar and flute and harmonica. I think I played harmonica first. Jews' harp and flutes. Things like that when I was a kid. And later on I got a hold of a guitar. I think my father's guitar was laying around the house. And we'd learn how to play and make all the changes. And they would call different boys in and teach them the changes. You know what I mean? And have them to play with us. So before long we had a little band and then we got a little larger band. And then we became known and we'd start playing at different affairs. How old were you then? Well as a time go along I guess I started at twelve so I must have been around fifteen or so. When we were really making headway and attracting attention. And so we were offered a job to play in the carnival parade for the Garden District Carnival Club. And they said if you can get a hold of a brass band and play as good as you do with your orchestra. Well we'll give you the job to the carnival. So we agreed to that. Well Tom and I were worried about getting uniforms to have for the men to play. So we joined the state militia. And we asked the captain to loan us the blue uniforms and the blue coats. And we got enough for the entire men. Ten men in this brass band. And everyone had to get white pants. See? And we had tan shoes and leggings. And freighting down the street we had the name of the band on top. See that covered the company's insignia. And we took off the cross guns. See? So we looked like we had band uniforms. Well the club at that particular year won first prize. And in the paper they mentioned how wonderful the band looked. You see? In the paper. So Tom didn't remember that. So I felt like going in the library and looking over the papers of that particular date. And see if I could get the clipping of that particular affair. So that was the first brass band affair that we played. And the club won first prize. And we had quite a nice mentioning about the band and how well we played.
